t: 3176. Find the Maximum Length of a Good Subsequence I
o: A good subsequence allows at most k adjacent unequal pairs. We pick elements (in index order) maximizing length subject to that budget. With n ≤ 500 and k ≤ 25, an O(n · D · k) DP over (last value taken, changes used) is easily fast enough. Example 1: taking 1,2,1,1 uses only 2 changes and gives length 4 (adding 3 would need a third). Example 2 with k=0 forces all-equal picks, so the best is any value twice.
k: DP state: best length ending with value v having used j changes.
Extending with the same value is free; switching values costs one change.
Only distinct values seen so far matter as 'last value' states.

a.n: Approach 1: DP keyed by last value
a.i: Maintain dp[v][j] = longest good subsequence (over processed prefix) ending in value v with exactly/at-most j changes. For each new x, the new best ending at x with j changes is max(dp[x][j] + 1, max over other values u of dp[u][j-1] + 1). Computing 'max over other values' by looping all distinct values is O(D) per element, giving O(n·D·k) ≤ ~6M operations.
s: Initialize empty map dp from value to array of size k+1.
For each x: gather best[j] = max dp[u][j] over u ≠ x.
Set ndp[x][j] = max(dp[x][j] + 1, best[j-1] + 1) and store.
Answer is the maximum over all dp entries.
a.t: O(n · D · k) where D ≤ n distinct values — about 6·10⁶ ops at the limits
a.sp: O(D · k) for the DP table

w: The exclusion of the current value when computing 'best other' is the main pitfall — forgetting it lets a value extend itself for free. An O(n·k) refinement tracks the top two dp maxima per change count (so the max excluding x is always available), which is the intended solution of the harder version II with n up to 10⁵. Edge cases: k = 0 (answer is the max frequency of any value... actually the longest run achievable via subsequence = highest frequency), and single-element arrays.
